data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli forces demolish five West Bank buildings and displace over 100 Palestinians
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Israeli forces demolish five West Bank buildings and displace over 100 Palestinians
Israeli forces demolished five Palestinian residential buildings in the occupied West Bank on Thursday without warning, displacing more than 100 people.
Troops raided the town of Biddu, northwest of Jerusalem, in the early morning, forcing residents of 12 apartments out before demolishing them.
Residents said soldiers fired stun grenades and tear gas at homeowners, preventing them from retrieving their belongings before the demolitions began.
The Jerusalem Governorate office has recorded a significant increase in demolitions and land-clearing operations in Jerusalem and its surrounding areas this year.
During the first nine months of 2026, it documented 427 operations, including 66 cases of forced self-demolition, in which Palestinians were compelled to tear down their own homes; 294 demolitions carried out using Israeli machinery; and 32 land-levelling operations.
In October alone, the office recorded a further 44 demolition and land-levelling operations, bringing the total number documented between January and the end of October to 471.

data.author: Mera Aladam

Israeli president Herzog deliberates after Eisenkot receives majority Knesset backing to become prime minister
Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot has received the backing of a majority of Knesset members to be prime minister, possibly granting him the mandate to attempt to form the next government.
Eisenkot received 67 recommendations compared with 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Yashar party urged Israeli president Isaac Herzog on Thursday to hand Eisenkot the mandate to form the next government "as soon as possible", adding that its the largest number of recommendations given to a candidate for forming a government since 2015.
"Benjamin Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister leading a minority of just 46 seats," the party said. "He has no mandate, no majority and no public trust."
While Herzog expressed that the result was "clear", he indicated that he would hold further talks with party leaders to clarify the situation before assigning the mandate to form a government on Sunday.

Iran’s Basij commander Hossein Taeb has said that the US and Israel are seeing change amid their ongoing attempts at transforming the Middle East's landscape.
"Today, we say that change has begun in America and Israel, and we will soon see it across different areas," he said during the closing ceremony of the 19th International Resistance Film Festival in Tehran.
His highlighted the use of media and film as a way of "disrupting America’s media monopoly", describing it as "resistance cinema".
"The staging of this festival under such circumstances signifies that - much like a combatant who never abandons their launchers during military defence - an artist engaged in the 'perceptual battlefield' does not desert their post, even under the shadow of war, economic siege, or any other threat," he said.
"Through their portrayal of the Resistance, they inflict a new defeat upon the enemy."
Referencing US-Israeli attacks on Gaza, Lebanon, Iraq and Syria, Taeb said: "All these crimes took place; children were killed, and the oppressed peoples of the region suffered. Yet, the true losers in this conflict were the United States and Israel."

data.title: Middle East Eye: Turkey moves closer to Saudi troop deployment as parliament approves Mecca defence pact
data.author: Ragip Soylu
data.summary:
Turkey moves closer to Saudi troop deployment as parliament approves Mecca defence pact
Submitted by
Ragip Soylu
on
Fri, 11/06/2026 - 09:04
Ankara must still secure a troop deployment mandate and finalise legal arrangements governing its forces in Saudi Arabia
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan (L), Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif posing after signing the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia (Handout/Pakistan prime minister's office/AFP)
Off
The Turkish parliament passed a law approving the Mecca defence pact early on Friday, completing a crucial stage in the legal process.
The bill was endorsed by 279 MPs, with 119 voting against it. It was primarily supported by the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and its coalition partner, the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP). However, the Republican People’s Party (CHP), a nominal opposition party, also backed the move.
Following the ousting of its leader through a court order, the CHP has split into two camps, and its new leadership is increasingly aligned with the Turkish government’s views.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is expected to publish the law in the Official Gazette later this week, bringing it into force.
Under the agreement, signed by regional powers Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August and submitted to parliament for approval last month, an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all.
The text of the agreement does not identify any specific country or region as a threat but emphasises that all participating countries will take the necessary measures to support one another in the event of an armed attack against their independence, sovereignty or territorial integrity.
The agreement, which consists of 16 articles, has no expiration date.

Iranians work on a section of a gas pipeline linking Iran and Pakistan after the project was launched during a ceremony in the Iranian border city of Chah Bahar on March 11, 2013. (ATTA KENARE / AFP)
Off
Turkey had to stop gas imports from Turkmenistan through Iran due to US pressure, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar revealed on Thursday during a briefing with journalists.
Ankara began receiving gas from Turkmenistan in March 2025 under a deal to supply 1.3 billion cubic metres annually using Iranian infrastructure.
Turkish gas importer Botas had an import licence for the arrangement until 2033.
Ashgabat cut the flow of gas in October 2025, at the time saying the two countries had a short-term contract and that, without an agreement on volumes or prices, it could not sell gas to Ankara.
Earlier this year, Bayraktar said gas imports from Turkmenistan via Iran would resume, but those plans did not materialise.
He has now revealed that the real problem was the US-Iran war, which started in February.
“We stopped because of the OFAC, (US Office of Foreign Assets Control), somehow involved in this,” he said.
“Although we were not paying anything to Iran, the situation escalated between Iran and the US.”

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'The alternative to diplomacy is war': Polisario warns of risks after collapse of Western Sahara UN mission
data.author: Alex MacDonald
data.summary:
'The alternative to diplomacy is war': Polisario warns of risks after collapse of Western Sahara UN mission
Submitted by
Alex MacDonald
on
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 12:17
Sahrawi administration’s top diplomat tells MEE that the US and European states have backed Morocco at the expense of their own interests and regional stability
A flag of the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic flutters at a security checkpoint outside the refugee camp of Dakhla, Algeria, on 14 January 2023 (Ryad Kramdi/AFP)
Off
Last week's failure by the UN Security Council to renew the mandate of its Western Sahara mission after 35 years has deepened concerns that the conflict could escalate militarily while slipping further from international attention.
The United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) was established in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front, the armed group fighting for Sahrawi independence in the territory, and pave the way for a referendum.
That ceasefire collapsed in 2020 and the referendum never happened.
Sunday appeared to be the final nail in the coffin for the peace process, with Minurso's mandate expiring after Russia and the US both vetoed each other's resolution to extend it.
The Polisario Front’s top diplomat told Middle East Eye that they were largely optimistic over the outcome as they had long viewed Minurso as ineffective at best and complicit with Morocco at worst.
The failed US resolution would have removed the word “referendum” from the mission’s name, changing it to the United Nations Mission in Western Sahara, and made Morocco's much-maligned "autonomy plan" for the Western Sahara the only basis for further progress.
'Now we are back to square one'
